name: Oral communication
intro: How to take part in discussions, ask follow-up questions, give presentations and use natural, idiomatic English when you speak.
sammendrag:
## Speaking with confidence

Speaking English is not about being perfect. It is about getting your message across, listening to others and keeping the conversation going. Many Norwegians understand English well but feel unsure when they speak. The best cure is practice – and some useful phrases.

## Taking part in a discussion

In a good discussion, people **listen**, **respond** to each other and **build on** what others say. Useful phrases:

- Giving your opinion: In my opinion…, I believe that…, As I see it…
- Agreeing: I agree with you. That's a good point. Exactly!
- Disagreeing politely: I see what you mean, but… I'm not sure I agree… That's true, however…
- Interrupting politely: Sorry to interrupt, but… Can I just add something?
- Asking for clarification: What do you mean by…? Could you give an example?

## Follow-up questions

**Follow-up questions** show that you are listening and help the conversation continue. Instead of just saying “OK”, ask: Why do you think so? How did that make you feel? What happened next? **Open questions** (starting with why, how, what) give longer answers than **closed questions** (yes/no).

## Presentations

A good presentation has a clear **structure**:

- **Introduction**: greet the audience, present your topic and tell them what you will talk about.
- **Main part**: two to four main points, with examples.
- **Conclusion**: sum up and thank the audience. Invite questions.

Use **signposting** to guide your listeners: First, I will talk about… Moving on to… Finally… Speak slowly and clearly, look at your audience, and use notes with keywords rather than reading a full script. Slides should support you, not replace you.

## Fluency and idiomatic English

**Fluency** means speaking smoothly without too many long pauses. **Fillers** like “well”, “you know” and “let me think” give you time without switching to Norwegian. **Idiomatic expressions** make your English sound natural: “It's up to you”, “to be honest”, “that makes sense”, “I'm on the fence” (I haven't decided).

Adapt your language to the situation. With friends you can be informal; in a job interview or formal debate, be more careful and polite.

## Pronunciation and clarity

Clear pronunciation matters more than a perfect accent. Stress important words, pause between ideas, and vary your intonation so you do not sound monotonous.

flashcards.def: A phrase for giving your opinion.

flashcards.term: I see what you mean, but…

flashcards.def: A phrase for asking for clarification.
A question that builds on what someone just said: Why do you think so?
A question starting with why, how or what, which invites a longer answer.
A question that can be answered with yes or no.
Phrases that guide listeners: First… Moving on to… Finally…
Short notes instead of a full script, so you can speak freely.
Speaking smoothly without too many long pauses.
Words like “well” and “let me think” that give you time to think.
I understand and agree with the logic.
The melody of speech. Varying it keeps listeners interested.

quiz.text: Which phrase is a polite way to disagree?
options: I see what you mean, but I'm not sure I agree.
quiz.explain: Acknowledging the other person's point before disagreeing keeps the discussion respectful.

options: Why do you think the law should change?
quiz.explain: Open questions start with words like why, how and what, and invite longer answers.

quiz.text: What is signposting in a presentation?
options: Phrases that guide the audience through your talk
quiz.explain: Phrases like “Moving on to…” help the audience follow your structure.

quiz.text: What does “I'm on the fence” mean?
quiz.explain: The idiom means you have not made up your mind.

options: They show you are listening and keep the conversation going
quiz.explain: Follow-up questions show interest and help the other person say more.

quiz.text: What is best to use as support during a presentation?
options: A full script you read word for word
quiz.explain: Keyword notes help you remember your points while still speaking freely to the audience.

quiz.text: Which phrase can you use to interrupt politely?
options: Sorry to interrupt, but can I add something?
quiz.explain: Apologising before interrupting is polite in English-speaking cultures.

options: Speaking smoothly without too many long pauses
quiz.explain: Fluency is about flow. You can be fluent and still have an accent.

quiz.text: What can you say to gain time when you need to think?
quiz.explain: Fillers like “well, let me think” keep the conversation going in English.

quiz.text: What should the conclusion of a presentation include?
options: A summary and a thank you, and an invitation for questions
quiz.explain: The conclusion wraps up and gives the audience a chance to ask questions.

ekstra.text: You must speak without any accent to communicate well in English.
ekstra.explain: Clarity matters more than accent. Many fluent speakers have an accent.

ekstra.text: “That's a good point” is a way of agreeing.
ekstra.explain: It shows that you appreciate what the other person said.

ekstra.text: Slides should replace what you say in a presentation.
ekstra.explain: Slides should support your talk, not replace it.

ekstra.text: “To be honest” is an idiomatic expression.
ekstra.explain: It is a common phrase used to introduce an honest opinion.
“Did you like the film?” can be answered with yes or no.

ekstra.text: What does “It's up to you” mean?
options: It is your turn to pay
ekstra.explain: “It's up to you” means the choice is yours.

options: Moving on to my second point…
ekstra.explain: “Moving on to…” tells the audience you are starting a new part.

skriv.text: Some people understand English well but feel unsure when they speak. Explain why practice can help, and what the main goal of speaking English is.
skriv.fasit: Practice helps you feel more confident when speaking. The goal is not to speak perfectly, but to get your message across, listen to others and keep the conversation going.
kriterier: Explains that practice can help with feeling unsure or speaking with confidence.
Explains that the aim is to communicate and take part in the conversation, not to be perfect.

skriv.text: Compare these questions: “Did you enjoy the presentation?” and “What did you think of the presentation?” Explain which is open and which is closed, and how the answers may differ.
skriv.fasit: “Did you enjoy the presentation?” is closed because it can be answered yes or no. “What did you think of the presentation?” is open and invites a longer answer.
kriterier: Identifies the yes-or-no question as closed and the other question as open.
Explains that an open question invites a longer answer than a closed question.

skriv.text: Your discussion partner says that only one person should speak in a group discussion. You disagree and think everyone should get a chance to speak. Write a polite response using “I see what you mean, but…”
skriv.fasit: I see what you mean, but I think everyone should get a chance to speak in a group discussion.
kriterier: Uses “I see what you mean, but…” to disagree politely.
Clearly expresses the view that everyone should have a chance to speak.

skriv.text: Explain how the introduction, main part and conclusion each help give a presentation a clear structure.
skriv.fasit: The introduction greets the audience, presents the topic and says what the presentation will cover. The main part develops the main points with examples, and the conclusion sums up the presentation.
kriterier: Explains the introduction’s role in introducing the topic and preparing the audience.
Explains that the main part develops points and that the conclusion sums things up.

skriv.text: You are preparing a presentation and have notes with only a few keywords. Explain why using these notes can be better than reading a full script.
skriv.fasit: Keyword notes help you speak more freely instead of reading every word. They remind you of your main ideas while allowing you to speak to the audience.
kriterier: Explains that keyword notes remind the speaker of important ideas.
Explains that notes allow the speaker to speak more freely than a full script.

skriv.text: A speaker talks very quickly and uses the same tone throughout a presentation. Suggest two changes that would make the speech clearer or more interesting for the audience.
skriv.fasit: The speaker should slow down and pause between ideas. They could also vary their intonation so the speech does not sound monotonous.
kriterier: Suggests speaking slowly or pausing between ideas to improve clarity.
Suggests varying intonation to make the speech less monotonous.

skriv.text: Explain how you might adapt your English when talking with friends and when speaking in a job interview.
skriv.fasit: With friends, you can use informal language. In a job interview, you should be more careful and polite.
kriterier: Describes friends as a situation where informal language is suitable.
Describes a job interview as a situation where more careful and polite language is suitable.

skriv.text: Your friend asks who should choose what you do after school. Reply using “It’s up to you” and explain what your reply means.
skriv.fasit: It’s up to you. That means you can decide what we do after school.
kriterier: Uses “It’s up to you” in a reply to the situation.
Explains that the friend is the one who gets to decide.
